title: Kernel Debugging with WinDbg
summary: With WinDbg attached to the lab VM (lesson 15.08), you can break into your driver's code, step through it, and inspect every kernel structure involved in a request. This lesson is a working session: breakpoints on driver load and on dispatch routines, debug output with levels, examining driver and device objects and IRPs with `!drvobj`, `!devobj` and `!irp`, and analysing a bug check your driver caused.
markdown:
## Before you start

- WinDbg on the host is connected to the VM's kernel (lesson 15.08) and the VM is running.
- Symbols: `.symfix` for Microsoft's, plus your build folder for the driver's PDB: `.sympath+ C:\code\XenonEcho\x64\Debug`, then `.reload`.
- Debug output enabled: `ed nt!Kd_DEFAULT_Mask 0xF` (or for `DbgPrintEx` with your own component and level, `ed nt!Kd_IHVDRIVER_Mask 0xF`).

## Breaking into your driver

| Goal | Command |
|---|---|
| Stop at `DriverEntry` before the driver is loaded | `bu XenonEcho!DriverEntry` (an unresolved breakpoint, placed when the module loads) |
| Stop in a dispatch routine | `bp XenonEcho!EchoDeviceControl` |
| Stop only for one control code | Set the breakpoint on a line inside that `case` (F9 in the source window), rather than on the function |
| Step over / into / out | `p` / `t` / `gu` |
| Show locals and parameters | `dv /t` |
| Show the call stack | `k` (`kP` with parameters) |
| Continue | `g` |
| Break in at any time | Ctrl+Break |

Start the driver in the VM (`sc start XenonEcho`); WinDbg stops at `DriverEntry`, and the entire VM freezes while you step through it. Then run the client (lesson 16.06) and stop in `EchoDeviceControl` for each request.

With the PDB loaded, WinDbg's source window follows along; the Locals and Call Stack panes behave like Visual Studio's (lesson 4.07).

## Looking at kernel structures

The `!` extensions understand the I/O manager's objects (lesson 15.05):

```
kd> !drvobj XenonEcho 7
Driver object (ffffa50c1a2b3e30) is for:  \Driver\XenonEcho
Device Object list:  ffffa50c19f0c8a0
...
Dispatch routines:
[00] IRP_MJ_CREATE              fffff8063f5e1010  XenonEcho!EchoCreateClose
[02] IRP_MJ_CLOSE               fffff8063f5e1010  XenonEcho!EchoCreateClose
[0e] IRP_MJ_DEVICE_CONTROL      fffff8063f5e1080  XenonEcho!EchoDeviceControl
...
kd> !devobj ffffa50c19f0c8a0
Device object (ffffa50c19f0c8a0) is for:  XenonEcho \Driver\XenonEcho DriverObject ffffa50c1a2b3e30
Current Irp 00000000 RefCount 1 Type 00008001 Flags 00000040
DevExt ffffa50c19f0c9f0 ...
```

- `!drvobj` shows the driver's devices and, with flag 7, its dispatch table: a quick check that `DriverEntry` filled it in correctly.
- `!devobj` shows a device's reference count (open handles, lesson 16.03), type (your `0x8001`) and extension.
- Inside a dispatch routine, `!irp @rdx` (the IRP is the second argument, so it is in `rdx` at the routine's first instruction, lesson 7.06) shows the request: major function, control code, buffer lengths, and the system buffer's address, which `db` can then dump.
- `dt XenonEcho!EchoState <address>` shows your device extension with field names, from the PDB.

## A bug check, end to end

Introduce a bug on purpose in the lab driver, for example reading the input header before checking its length in a copy of lesson 16.07's handler, and send it a 1-byte request. With Driver Verifier's special pool on (lesson 15.07), the read past the system buffer faults at once. WinDbg breaks in with the bug check; then:

```
kd> !analyze -v
...
PAGE_FAULT_IN_NONPAGED_AREA (50)
Invalid system memory was referenced. ...
FAULTING_SOURCE_LINE:  C:\code\XenonEcho\dispatch.cpp
FAULTING_SOURCE_LINE_NUMBER:  48
...
STACK_TEXT:
XenonEcho!EchoReadRecords+0x1a
XenonEcho!EchoDeviceControl+0x6c
nt!IofCallDriver+0x55
nt!IopSynchronousServiceTail+0x1a8
nt!IopXxxControlFile+0x5e5
nt!NtDeviceIoControlFile+0x56
nt!KiSystemServiceCopyEnd+0x25
ntdll!NtDeviceIoControlFile+0x14
KERNELBASE!DeviceIoControl+0x6b
EchoClient!wmain+0x84
```

That one stack is the whole of chapters 15 and 16: the client's `DeviceIoControl`, the system call (lesson 15.02), the I/O manager building and dispatching the IRP (lesson 15.05), and your dispatch routine at the line that read too far. Fix the check, rebuild, revert the VM to the snapshot if needed, and test again.

## Common mistakes

> [!warning] Breakpoints that never hit
> Check symbols with `lm v m XenonEcho` and that the loaded driver is the build whose PDB you gave WinDbg.

> [!warning] Forgetting the debug output mask
> `KdPrint` output is filtered until the mask is set.

> [!warning] Leaving the VM frozen
> While stopped in the debugger the whole guest is frozen: continue with `g` when done.

## Check yourself
```quiz
? How do you see a driver's dispatch table in WinDbg?
+ `!drvobj <name> 7`
- `lm m XenonEcho`
- `k` while inside `DriverEntry`
- `dt _DRIVER_OBJECT` with no address
> It lists the driver's device objects and the routine for each IRP major function.

? Where is the IRP when a dispatch routine starts, and how do you look at it?
- In `rcx`; `dt _IRP @rcx`
- On the top of the stack; `dq @rsp`
- In a global variable named `Irp`
+ In `rdx`; look with `!irp @rdx`
> A dispatch routine's arguments are the device object (`rcx`) and the IRP (`rdx`).

? What does a bug check's stack show for a request from user mode?
+ The path from the client, through the kernel, to the driver
- Only the driver's own functions
- The client program's source code
- The order in which drivers were loaded
> Frames such as `nt!NtDeviceIoControlFile` mark where the request entered the kernel.

? Why use `bu` rather than `bp` for `DriverEntry`?
+ It resolves when the driver loads
- `bp` does not work in the kernel
- `bu` is faster
> Unresolved breakpoints wait for the module.

? What does `!drvobj XenonEcho 7` show?
- The driver's source code
+ Its devices and dispatch routines
- All IRPs in the system
> A quick check that DriverEntry set things up correctly.

? In the bug check stack, what does `nt!NtDeviceIoControlFile` represent?
- A function in the driver
- The client program
+ The kernel side of the system call
> Lesson 15.02's path, seen in a real stack.
```
ideas:
- Break at `DriverEntry`, step through it, then run `!drvobj XenonEcho 7` after it returns.
- Stop in `EchoDeviceControl`, run `!irp @rdx`, and dump the system buffer with `db`.
- Introduce the deliberate bug, enable Verifier for the driver, trigger it, and read `!analyze -v`.
